title: Service
hookLine: practice turned outward: time given to others
tomorrow: who washed the sick monk nobody would touch?

lines: A MURAL AT A YOUTH CENTER.
cards: Put your own oxygen mask on first: anyone who's flown has heard it. Mai's summer program has a community art day this weekend, painting a mural at a youth center, and she almost skipped the sign-up.
Her reason: she can barely sit through the chanting without fidgeting, so who is she to help anyone? Inside the Buddhist texts, both sides of her argument have a voice.

teach.b: The first voice is in the Dhammapada: let each person first set himself in what is right, and only then teach others; that way the wise won't come to grief. Its case is real.
Help from someone who hasn't tamed their own anger can do harm, and you can't give what you don't have. The second voice is in the Vinaya.

teach.h: GO, FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.
teach.b: Soon after his awakening, the Buddha sends his first disciples out to wander for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world. Its case is real too.
The world won't wait for anyone to be finished, and those disciples were sent out while they were still new. Both are scripture, and Buddhists hold them together in their own ways.
In the Mahayana schools, including the Vietnamese temples of Mai's family, the ideal is the bodhisattva, who vows to keep working for the freedom of all beings.

teach.h: THE BODHISATTVA'S VOW; THE ALMS ROUND.
teach.b: In Theravada lands, monks walk for alms each morning and lay people serve by feeding them, and both the giving and the receiving count as practice.
Either way, service isn't an extra after the real work.
It's practice turned outward: time and hands given to others, while the training goes on.

how: Buddhists serve through temple work, feeding monks on their alms rounds, and volunteering in their wider communities; in Mahayana traditions the bodhisattva vow to work for the freedom of all beings frames service as part of the path.

o: a fee lay people pay to support their local temple
practice turned outward: time and hands given to others
chores a novice monk must finish before he meditates

games.q: two voices on serving — tap the pairs.
p: set yourself right, then teach others
go, for the good of the many
vows to work for all beings

s: Buddhism teaches you must be fully awakened before helping anyone
the Buddha sent his disciples out while they were new, for the good of the many.
the Dhammapada has a verse about setting yourself right before teaching others
that's the first voice, and its case is real: you can't give what you don't have.
in Mahayana schools the bodhisattva vows to work for the freedom of all beings
it's the ideal in the Vietnamese temples of Mai's family.

games.q: Mai's roommate says you can't serve anyone until you've fixed yourself. give that view its best case, in one line.
o: help from someone who hasn't tamed their own anger can do real harm.
helping others distracts you from what really matters: your own freedom.
the Buddha never asked his followers to do anything for other people.
games.why: that's the Dhammapada's real point: set yourself right first. the Vinaya adds the other voice: go out, for the good of the many, while still new.

practice: Count on your fingers the people whose service you used today without thinking: whoever grew your breakfast, drove the bus, cleaned the floor, answered a question. One finger for each.
Then rest your hands in your lap and stay with them while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Service: practice turned outward, your time and hands given to others while your own training goes on.

orig.note: Pali: for the good of the many; from the words sending the first disciples out.

carryVoice: Your line: outward. Nobody in the Vinaya waited to be finished first. Twenty-one days into the block.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga I.11.1 (the disciples sent out to wander)
